evidence: Paul. ex Fest. p. 35 Müll.: bilinguēs Bruttātēs Ennius dīxit, quod Bruttiī et Oscē et Graecē loquī solitī sint (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The word Ennius used of the Bruttians, who spoke Oscan and Greek, and Horace of a man of Canusium, a town that spoke Greek and Oscan, mixing his words. It also means double-tongued, deceitful (Verg. A. 1.661 Tyriōsque bilinguīs; see “deceitful”), so where praise is meant, say it with utraque lingua: Pliny’s friend utrāque linguā valet.

terms.gloss: be at home in both languages
evidence: Plin. Ep. 7.25.4: Nam tantum utrāque linguā valet

terms.gloss: of both languages (Greek and Latin): learned in both, the authors of both
evidence: Hor. C. 3.8.5: docte sermōnēs utrīusque linguae
Suet. Aug. 89.1: in ēvolvendīs utrīusque linguae auctōribus

phrases.latin: Hic puer bilinguis est: cum mātre aliā linguā, mēcum Latīnē loquitur.
phrases.english: This boy is bilingual: he speaks another language with his mother and Latin with me.

phrases.latin: Quam tersa omnia, quam Latīna, quam Graeca! Nam tantum utrāque linguā valet, ut ea magis videātur excellere, quā cum maximē loquitur.
phrases.english: How polished everything was, how Latin, how Greek! For he is so strong in both languages that whichever he is speaking at the moment seems the one he is better at.

phrases.latin: patriīs intermiscēre petīta verba forīs mālīs, Canusīnī mōre bilinguis
phrases.english: would you rather mix words fetched from abroad with your native ones, like a two-tongued man of Canusium?

sources: Lewis & Short: bilinguis · Lewis & Short: lingua
